catalog_quote: Rottland 1982:78 (5.1.3.2 Druckakzent): "Tucker/Bryan und Tucker sprechen in allen Arbeiten zum Kalenjin von 'stressed syllables', 'shift in stress' usw.; der Druckakzent scheint aber nach ihren Angaben mit Hochton oder Steigton korreliert zu sein, und markiert werden bei ihnen nur die Tonhöhen. In Heines Sogoo-Vokabular sind Druckakzent und Tonhöhe unabhängig bezeichnet (Heine 1973). Der Druckakzent geht hier mit hohem oder mit fallendem Ton einher, ist aber weiter nicht vorhersagbar. Bei meinen Aufzeichnungen habe ich keine Anzeichen für Druckakzent in phonemischer Funktion feststellen können und bezeichne ihn deshalb nicht. Phonetisch sind betonte Silben erkennbar, und zwar immer in Verbindung mit nicht-tiefem Ton." || Jerono 2011:36: "Tugen is a tonal language in the sense that tone is used to differentiate lexical items. A lexeme such as pis has two meanings depending on the tonal pattern. ... However, Tugen is not a typical tone language in that not every lexeme has different tones. ... Tugen on the other hand has two underlying tones namely: H(igh) and L(ow) tones." || Lodge 1995:31: "Kalenjin is a tone language, but whether the tonal system interacts with the harmony system is not clear, so I have not included tonal markings in the transcriptions"

new_statements.translation: Tucker/Bryan and Tucker speak in all their works on Kalenjin of 'stressed syllables', 'shift in stress', etc.; but by their own account the stress accent seems to be correlated with high or rising tone, and they mark only the pitch levels. [...] In my recordings I could find no sign of stress accent in a phonemic function, and therefore I do not mark it. Phonetically, stressed syllables are recognisable, and always in conjunction with non-low tone.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Named file contains the quoted 5.1.3.2 'Druckakzent' text exactly as reported (the report's '[..]' elides the two Heine/Sogoo sentences, which the file has). I re-parsed the six raw Google Books Atom feeds in gbfeeds/ (........): every fragment is there verbatim under volumes uzwaAQAAIAAJ / 0ocOAAAAYAAJ, 'Die südnilotischen Sprachen / Franz Rottland / 1982', with overlapping joins ('korreliert zu sein', 'fallendem Ton einher', 'keine Anzeichen.. Phonetisch sind betonte', 'nicht-tiefem Ton. 5.1.3.3 Ton'). Differences from the raw snippets are only line-break hyphens removed (syl-lables, Ton-höhen, bezeich-ne, nicht - tiefem) and quote-mark normalisation. No page scan or page-labelled snippet…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kalenjin (Tugen included) is a tone language (H/L; Jerono 2011 for Tugen). Rottland finds no phonemic word stress; a phonetic prominence is audible and always sits on a syllable bearing a non-low (high or falling) tone, i.e. stress, where heard, is a correlate of tone rather than an independent positional rule. No source gives a syllable-position rule for Tugen.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Rottland notes that in Heine's Sogoo (Okiek) vocabulary stress and tone are marked independently, stress going with high or falling tone but 'otherwise not predictable' — that remark concerns Sogoo, not Tugen. Tugen-specific sources: Jerono 2011:36-37 'Tugen is a tonal language.. However, Tugen is not a typical tone language in that not every lexeme has different tones' (silent on stress); Lodge 1995:31 (Tugen informant) 'Kalenjin is a tone language' (silent on stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Rottland's remark concerns word-level 'Druckakzent' in isolated forms from his own recordings across Kalenjin varieties; it names no domain explicitly. It is a pan-Kalenjin statement in a comparative monograph, not a Tugen-specific one, and its text here is re-assembled from six overlapping Google Books API snippets (verbatim, but no page scan). Tugen-specific descriptions (Jerono 2011 ch. 2; Lodge 1995; Local & Lodge 1996) are consistent with it: tone language, stress never mentioned.
new_statements.identity_note: The stress statement is Rottland 1982's pan-Kalenjin one (ch. 5 'Kalenjin' describes the whole Kalenjin cluster; Tugen = Rottland's 'Tugen/Tukin/Tugin, Kamasia', p.21), not a Tugen-only description; Tugen-specific sources (Jerono 2011, Lodge 1995 with a Tugen informant, Local & Lodge 1996 with Tugen speakers) describe a H/L tone language and never mention stress. Jerono 2011 treats Tugen as 'one of the dialects within the Kalenjin macro-language'; Lodge 1995 calls it 'the Tugen dialect' of Kalenjin. Glottolog language-level code tuge1241 [tuy]. The catalog already carries the sister language Nandi (nand1266) on the Harvard library catalogue 1909 + Lodge 1995; the Rottland passage applies to that entry as well.

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog's tonal record and with Rottland 1982:78, who reports that Tucker speaks of 'stressed syllables' and 'shift in stress' in his Kalenjin work while marking only pitch: the fragments show exactly that usage ('shift in stress', 'when stressed/unstressed', 'governed by stress') next to a tone-mark inventory. They add the first-hand detail that Tucker ties vowel length/shortening to stress and that stress shifts between Primary and Secondary noun forms; they do not give a placement rule, so nothing contradicts or sharpens the catalog's 'tonal, stress phonetic and not shown to be phonemic' reading. Statement is pan-Kalenjin (Nandi-Kipsigis, Pakot), not Tugen-specific.
new_statements.rule_in_words: From the reachable fragments only: Tucker describes Kalenjin (Nandi-Kipsigis and Pakot data; Tugen named as a Nandi-group member) with five tone marks (High, Low, Mid, Falling, Rising) and treats stress as a real phonetic factor that shifts between morphological forms of a word: half-long syllables are 'inherently long syllables affected by shift in stress' (Nandi primary kimagé:t vs secondary kimagé'tyét), Pakot short /i u e o/ occur only as stress-governed shortenings of long vowels, and /ɔ:/ has different quality stressed vs unstressed. No sentence saying where word stress falls, or whether it is predictable, was reachable; a dedicated stress paragraph may exist between para 17 and 'Tone 19.' or after it but could not be surfaced.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker 1964 describes Kalenjin from Nandi-Kipsigis and Pakot (Pokot) data; Tugen ('Kamasia') is only listed as a member of the Nandi group, so any stress statement in it is pan-Kalenjin, not Tugen-specific (as is the catalog's Rottland 1982 statement).

tone_statements.summary: Tugen (with Nandi and Keyo) has four surface tones derived from three underlying tonemes H, L and Falling on nouns; no downdrift and no automatic downstep after L; the low-falling tone lowers the register of following tones.
